 What's happening now
 • Nationwide ground stop: Major airlines could shut down for the evening , a source tells CNN, after federal officials halted all US flight departures due to safety concerns from a telecommunications outage . The issue stems from a problem with network routers that cascaded nationwide, an airline source said.
 • Travel nightmare: Airlines and passengers are figuring out their next steps as thousands of flights are delayed or canceled. The skies are emptying as flights that were already in the air come in for landing.
 • No timetable for resolution: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned that there’s no known time frame for resolving the issue and that he expects an extended process.
 • No known threat: Mullin said the ground stop did not stem from a threat to the US and was not linked to this week’s disruptive Microsoft outage. Preliminary reports indicate this was not a cyberattack , law enforcement sources told CNN. President Donald Trump has been briefed .

 "Very old and antiquated" tech may be to blame, former transportation secretary says
 By Dalia Faheid 
 “Very old and antiquated” technology that air traffic controllers use to guide planes in and out of airports may have contributed to the nationwide meltdown today, former Secretary of Transportation Ray LaHood told CNN affiliate WEEK.
 “I assume that there’s been some serious glitch with that technology,” he told WEEK from Peoria International Airport in Illinois.
 Specifically, LaHood said there was likely an issue at the Potomac Consolidated TRACON (Terminal Radar Approach Control), the main TRACON facility outside of Washington, DC.
 “That’s kind of the heartbeat of this technology,” he said. “That’s the place where you have people watching planes being guided in and out of airports all over the country, and I assume something happened there.”
 LaHood called the ground stop “a national calamity.”
 “Thousands of people are relying on getting on an airplane and it’s kind of incomprehensible to think that this could happen in the 21st century.”

 FAA nationwide ground stop throws many of Saturday's sports games into question
 By Jacob Lev 
 With the FAA ordering a nationwide ground stop, sports in all leagues and competitions could be impacted on Saturday.
 According to ESPN’s Pete Thamel , many college football teams are having flight issues, including No. 6 Texas, No. 8 Tennessee and No. 19 Ole Miss.
 The SEC said it is “aware” of the ground stop and remains “in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses.”
 Many other teams in the Big 12 and Big Ten are also have reported issues.
 “Due to the national FAA ground stop impacting team travel, the Big 12 Conference is evaluating potential changes to Saturday’s football schedule,” the conference said in a statement to CNN. “The Conference will continue to monitor the travel disruptions alongside its member institutions and provide updates for Saturday’s games.”
 CNN has reached out to the Big Ten for comment but did not immediately hear back.
 There are also five National Basketball Association (NBA) games and 14 National Hockey League (NHL) games scheduled for Saturday.
 CNN has reached out to the NBA and NHL for comment.
 The NFL told CNN that all teams are scheduled to travel on Saturday and the Detroit Lions and New England Patriots are already in Munich, Germany ahead of their international game at the Allianz Arena on Sunday.

 Faced with no other options, travelers at Miami airport find out they can’t fly
 By Carolina Peguero and Emma Tucker 
 People wait in a check-in line at the British Airways counter in Miami International Airport after the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop on Friday, in Miami, Florida. 
 Joe Raedle/Getty Images 
 There was still a sense of calm among travelers arriving at Miami International Airport as they began to navigate the ramifications of a nationwide ground stop on all departures.
 People have been learning of the news after trying to check in for their flights. Some are walking up and down hallways trying to figure out their next steps. Others have already been waiting at the airport for a few hours, realizing they have no other options to get to their destinations.
 At the American Airlines information desks, workers are helping passengers understand what options they might have. Travelers holding their suitcases who had connecting flights, hoping to head on to international destinations, have eventually realized their plans wouldn’t pan out how they expected.
 One traveler named Chelsea, who was with her children, told CNN she was planning to surprise them with their destination point. She found out about the advisory as her husband was returning their rental car.
 Their flight went from delayed to canceled.
 “No rental cars, no hotels with shuttles. … Just trying to find a solution at this point,” Chelsea said.
 The family is “very disappointed,” she told CNN, adding that her children didn’t know where they were headed but found out from announcements at the airport that their flights had been impacted.

 Flights within Alaska and Hawaii can still depart, airlines say
 By Tori B. Powell 
 The nationwide ground stop currently in effect won’t affect the country’s noncontiguous states, according to Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.
 The airlines said that flights within Alaska, nearby neighboring islands, and Hawaii, as well as flights from the West Coast to Hawaii and international flights from Honolulu, can still depart.
 “Because of the significance of the ground stop, we have canceled some flights and diverted others,” Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines said in a statement. “When the ground stop is lifted, it will take time for our operations to get back on track for the rest of the day.”
 Pacific-bound flights have been cleared to depart from San Francisco International Airport, the airport said in a post on social media today.

 Here’s why US authorities have — so far — concluded aviation incident was not an attack
 By Josh Campbell 
 A “whole of government” response to Friday’s incident involving national air traffic by multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies has still not identified a nefarious attack, a senior US security source told CNN.
 Authorities continue to believe the issue was caused by a communication software issue rather than an intentional act, the source said, even as cyber specialists coast to coast are still investigating the incident.
 US law enforcement and intelligence agencies began receiving internal updates from aviation officials notifying them something was amiss right around when television screens inside agencies’ 24-hour command centers in the agencies’ headquarters began alerting officials to the issue Friday.
 It prompted officials at the FBI, Department of Homeland Security, and even the US National Security Agency — which leads efforts to counter foreign cyber threats — to spring into action.
 “Still no indication this was an attack,” the senior security source said late Friday. The source added the collective security response included “drilling down on” the various means the US government’s aviation system connects to networks that could potentially be exposed to bad actors.
 The source said efforts by US security services to identify any potential “node of attack” are expected to continue “at full speed” in the coming days, as cyber threats can sometimes eventually be located deep inside computer networks.

 Traveler opts for 6-hour drive to Montreal instead of waiting out ground stop in Newark
 By Brian Stelter 
 Yehya Siddiqui, 37, saw the news of the ground stop while waiting at Newark airport for a flight home to Montreal.
 His first thought? “Everybody’s going to be renting cars,” he said. Siddiqui, who was visiting New York for client meetings, booked a rental SUV immediately, and now he’s planning to drive across the border to Canada. 
First, though, he said he’ll stop in Albany, New York to sleep for the night.
Siddiqui was originally supposed to fly home on Thursday, but thunderstorms scuttled that flight, and he was rebooked for Friday.
 “I don’t know how long the FAA will shut this down,” he said, so he’s opting to drive the six and a half hours home instead.
 At Newark airport, a long line of people walked toward the rental car counters around 6:30 p.m. ET, hoping cars would still be available.

 Here’s what we know (and don’t know) about the ground stop affecting the nation so far
 By Tori B. Powell 
 The Federal Aviation Administration announced this afternoon “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety” prompted a ground stop for all flights in the United States.
 Here’s what we know so far and outstanding questions left to be answered: 
 What is a ground stop?: A ground stop is an order issued by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which requires aircraft to remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in flight are allowed to remain in the air.
 Unclear cause: The reason for the ground stop was not immediately clear , but an FAA spokesperson said there is a communications problem affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle flights going across the country. According to Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy, “FAA technicians are investigating the issue .” But preliminary reports indicate this is not a cyberattack, according to two law enforcement officials. The FAA “doesn’t know yet what is going on; it is affecting different facilities in different ways,” an airline source told CNN. “Ten minutes ago, they were on a crisis call and there was still no clear answer as to a cause.”
 DHS weighs in: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says there is currently no reason to suspect a national security threat is behind the outage that grounded all US flights. He did say the department is looking into whether a new AI-supported air traffic control system contributed to massive communications problems, though. Mullin also said yesterday’s massive global Microsoft outage and today’s problem causing the ground stop are not connected . He added officials have not yet discussed a time frame for resolving the outage as the administration focuses on passenger safety.
 Briefing: President Donald Trump has been briefed by officials on the FAA ground stop, Mullin said, adding he has spoken on the phone with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
 Ground stop history: The last time there was a nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, when a pilot notification system went down. Prior to that, the last nationwide ground stop was issued after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
 What people are saying: Airlines for America, the major trade association representing US airlines, said it’s in close communication with the Department of Transportation and the FAA. Major airlines, including American , United and Southwest , have notified passengers of the ground stop. And Sen. Tammy Duckworth today called for a “thorough and complete” investigation into the matter. See how travelers and pilots are reacting to the ground stop here. 
 CNN’s Pete Muntean, Aaron Cooper, Evan Perez, Hannah Rabinowitz, Nicki Brown, Brian Stelter, Kevin Liptak, Molly English, Dalia Faheid, Emma Tucker and Aleena Fayaz contributed reporting.

 Trump’s top aides monitoring and seeking answers over nationwide groundstop
 By Kaitlan Collins 
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth were both in and out of the West Wing Friday as officials scrambled to respond to a nationwide ground stop of flights.
 Hegseth was in the Situation Room, a person familiar with the matter told CNN, as Mullin briefly stepped outside to answer reporters’ questions.
 Mullin said President Donald Trump had been briefed by officials on the FAA ground stop for all flights and had spoken on the phone with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
 That urgency wasn’t apparent across government social media accounts, namely the president’s.
 The president posted on Truth Social about an effort to provide tax incentives to help revitalize the US entertainment industry, and about a Coast Guard rescue from a crash between two ships in Louisiana.

 Baby all done after family stuck at airport in Chicago 
 0:32
 A mother and her 21-month-old daughter have been stranded at Chicago O’Hare International Airport for about 9 hours, she told CNN.
 “All done,” her exhausted toddler repeated to her mom, Melissa Ogden.
 “She’s very tired of this day,” Ogden said.
 Ogden said she had been at the airport since 8 a.m. for her 10:30 a.m. flight to San Francisco, where she was traveling for work.
 “Then we went through security and did all of the normal stuff, and then got on the plane, and then yeah, it took forever,” she said.
 She was told their bags would be transported there without them.
 Ogden said she hasn’t yet rebooked the flight for a later date.
 “We just wait and see, because I mean there’s no way that if they get all this stuff figured out that a flight is going to go anytime soon,” she said. “There’s going to be a cascading effect.”
 For now, she’s just grateful her family is safe.
 “We’re just going to go home and just hope that everything gets better and it’s not a big deal,” she said.
